candidates.title: Subpart CC — Petroleum Refineries

criteria.criterion: if the plant site is a major source as defined in CAA section 112(a) and the process unit emits or contains one or more hazardous air pollutants listed in table 1 of this subpart then this subpart CC applies to the petroleum refining process unit and related emission points

if a vent stream has a total organic HAP concentration greater than or equal to 20 parts per million by volume and total VOC emissions at the outlet prior to control are greater than or equal to 33 kilograms per day for an existing source (or 6.8 kilograms per day for a new source) then that vent is a Group 1 miscellaneous process vent

if an owner or operator elects to control a Group 1 miscellaneous process vent with a control device (other than a flare meeting §63.670 requirements) then the control must reduce organic HAP emissions by 98 weight-percent or to a concentration of 20 parts per million by volume (dry, corrected to 3 percent oxygen), whichever is less stringent

if a Group 1 miscellaneous process vent uses a combustion device to comply with §63.643(a) then the owner or operator shall install, calibrate, maintain, and operate the monitoring equipment specified in §63.644(a) unless an exemption in §63.644(a) applies or an alternative monitoring approval under §63.644(b) is obtained

if the owner or operator uses a control device other than an incinerator, boiler, process heater, or flare, or uses one of those listed devices but seeks to monitor a parameter other than those specified in §63.644(a) then the owner or operator must request approval to monitor other parameters according to the procedures in §63.655(h)

if a vent system contains bypass lines that could divert a Group 1 vent stream away from the control device used to comply with §63.643(a) then the owner or operator must comply with one of the options in §63.644(c) (install an hourly flow indicator or continuously monitored valve position indicator, secure the bypass with a car-seal or lock-and-key and perform monthly visual inspections, or use a cap/blind flange/plug/second valve per referenced §60.482-6 requirements)

if a process vent is used only as a result of startup, shutdown, maintenance, or inspection and meets the conditions in §63.643(c) then the owner or operator may designate it as a maintenance vent and be required only to comply with the maintenance vent provisions in §63.643(c) and the specified reporting paragraphs

if the control device is a boiler or process heater with design heat input capacity greater than or equal to 44 megawatts or if all vent streams are introduced into the flame zone then monitoring under §63.644(a) is not required for that device

if the control device is a boiler or process heater with design heat input capacity less than 44 megawatts and the vent stream is not introduced into the flame zone then a firebox temperature monitoring device with a continuous recorder is required as specified in §63.644(a)(4)

checklist: Confirm whether the plant site is a major source under CAA section 112(a).

Confirm that the orthoxylene rerun column and associated vent are part of a petroleum refining process unit subject to Subpart CC (e.g., SIC 2911 or meeting the petroleum refining process unit definition).
Measure or calculate the vent outlet total organic HAP concentration (ppmv, dry) to determine whether it is ≥20 ppmv.
Measure or calculate total VOC organic HAP emissions at the outlet prior to control (kg/day) to determine Group 1 thresholds (≥33 kg/day for existing sources or ≥6.8 kg/day for new sources).
Determine whether the vent stream is routed to a refinery fuel gas system (if routed to fuel gas system, check §63.640(d)(5) and later flare §63.670 applicability).
Identify whether the source is an existing vs. new source (to apply correct Group 1 emissions thresholds and compliance dates).

Identify the control device type planned or in use for the vent (flare, incinerator/catalytic incinerator, boiler, process heater, or other) and confirm whether the device will be used to achieve ≥98 wt-% reduction or ≤20 ppmv (dry, corrected to 3% O2).
If using a combustion device, determine applicable monitoring requirements per §63.644(a) for that device and whether any exemptions (e.g., boilers ≥44 MW or vent introduced into flame zone) apply.

If you plan different monitoring parameters than those listed in §63.644(a) or will use a control device other than incinerator/boiler/process heater/flare, prepare and be ready to submit an alternative monitoring approval request per §63.655(h).

Check whether the vent is only used during startup/shutdown/maintenance/inspection and, if so, evaluate whether the criteria in §63.643(c)(1)–(5) (e.g., <10% LEL, ≤5 psig, <72 lb VOC, pyrophoric exceptions) can be met to qualify as a maintenance vent.

Inspect the vent system for bypass lines that could divert vent streams from the control device and prepare to implement one of the §63.644(c) options (hourly flow indicator/continuously monitored valve position; car-seal/lock-and-key with monthly inspection; or cap/blind flange/plug/second valve) and associated recordkeeping.

Prepare monitoring, recordkeeping, and reporting documentation consistent with §63.644 and the tables in the Subpart CC appendix (e.g., continuous recorder outputs, hourly pilot flame records, daily averages, NCS and periodic report contents) and the submission route per §63.655(h)/(i).

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants: Hazardous Waste Combustors (Subpart EEE)

criteria.criterion: If you seek to waive an operating parameter limit specified in this subpart, then you must submit an application to the Administrator showing that neither that operating parameter limit nor an alternative operating parameter limit is needed to ensure compliance with the emission standards of this subpart.

If you submit an application to waive an operating parameter limit, then the application must be submitted not later than with the comprehensive performance test plan and must include data or information justifying the request (for example technical or economic infeasibility or impracticality) and a description of the proposed alternative monitoring or justification for waiver.

If you request approval of an alternative monitoring requirement or waiver, then the Administrator will approve the request only if the alternative provides equivalent or better assurance of compliance with the relevant emission standard or is the monitoring requirement that best assures compliance and is technically and economically practicable.

If your combustor operates a hazardous waste firing system, then you must specify operating parameters and establish limits during the comprehensive performance test to ensure good operation of each hazardous waste firing system.

If your comprehensive performance test plan is prepared, then it must include an analysis of each feedstream that at minimum documents heating value, levels of relevant constituents, and viscosity or a description of the feedstream's physical form (e.g., wastes fed by simple lances).

If your combustor is equipped with a low-energy wet scrubber to control hydrogen chloride and chlorine gas, then you must establish and comply with a minimum liquid feed pressure based on manufacturer specifications as an hourly rolling average unless you obtain an approved waiver or alternative monitoring under § 63.1209(g)(1).

If you propose to waive monitoring of liquid feed pressure or other scrubber parameters, then your application must describe the proposed alternative monitoring approach (including operating parameter to be monitored, detector type and location, averaging period, and how the limit will be calculated) and include data showing the alternative would provide equivalent or better assurance of compliance.

checklist: Confirm the unit is an affected hazardous waste combustor (hazardous waste incinerator) subject to Subpart EEE.
Identify whether the wet scrubber for HCl/Cl2 is high-energy (e.g., venturi) or low-energy (e.g., spray tower, packed bed, tray tower).

Determine whether a minimum liquid feed pressure for the wet scrubber was established in the comprehensive performance test or in the Notification of Compliance and whether it is based on manufacturer specifications.
Assemble the comprehensive performance test plan and confirm the planned submittal timing (waiver/alternative requests must be submitted no later than with this plan).

Prepare feedstream analyses for wastes fed via lances including heating value, chlorine content, other relevant constituents, and viscosity or physical form documentation per the performance test plan requirements.

Document the firing system operating parameters currently used or measured (e.g., waste viscosity, delivery pressure, atomization pressure, feedrate ranges) and whether limits were established from prior performance testing.

Collect data and rationale to justify technical or economic infeasibility of the specific operating-parameter monitoring or to demonstrate that an alternative monitoring approach provides equivalent or better assurance of compliance.
Define the proposed alternative monitoring approach (parameter to monitor, detector type, monitoring location, averaging period, calculation method) to include in the waiver application.

Verify whether Automatic Waste Feed Cutoff (AWFCO) interlocks are required or currently linked to the parameter(s) in question and document how a waiver would affect AWFCO logic and protective actions.
Confirm the Administrator's approval criteria and be prepared for the Administrator to deny the waiver unless the alternative provides equivalent assurance of compliance.

candidates.title: Subpart EEEEE — Iron and Steel Foundries

criteria.criterion: If you have an existing affected source, then you must comply with each emissions limitation, work practice standard, and operation and maintenance requirement in this subpart no later than April 23, 2007.
If you are required to conduct a performance test for initial compliance, then you must conduct the performance test no later than 180 calendar days after the compliance date specified in § 63.7683.

If you conduct a performance test for initial compliance, then the test must be conducted under conditions representative of normal operations (excluding startup, shutdown, and periods of malfunction) and you must record process information to document that the operating conditions during the test represent normal operation.
If you plan to conduct a performance test, then you must submit a notification of intent to conduct the performance test at least 60 calendar days before the performance test is scheduled to begin.

If you conduct a PM performance test for a pouring station or pouring area, then you must follow the procedures in § 63.7732(b) including using the specified Method 1/1A and Method 5 (or other listed methods), collecting a minimum sample volume of 60 dscf per PM run, and obtaining at least three valid test runs (and calculate mass-based rates using the specified equation when applicable).

If you intend to use a performance test as your initial compliance demonstration, then the performance test results must meet the applicable numeric emissions limits or alternatives listed in § 63.7734(a) for the applicable source type (e.g., pouring station or pouring area at an existing or new foundry).

If you want the test production rates to be considered representative of current capabilities for the initial compliance demonstration, then you must have recorded the total mass of metal charged during each test run and other process information during the test to support that those operating/production conditions represented normal operation.

If you completed a performance test and are using it for initial compliance, then you must submit the notification of compliance status including the performance test results before the close of business on the 60th calendar day following completion of the performance test.

checklist: Confirm whether your foundry is an existing or new affected source and the facility startup date relative to April 22, 2004 (to establish the applicable compliance date) (40 CFR 63.7683).

Record the exact date(s) of the April 2005 M-1 Pouring Area performance test and compare to the compliance date (April 23, 2007) and the 180-day post-compliance-date testing window (40 CFR 63.7683(a); 40 CFR 63.7730(a)).
Verify whether you submitted a Notification of Intent to conduct the performance test at least 60 calendar days before the April 2005 test (40 CFR 63.7750(d)).

Assemble test documentation showing that each performance test run was conducted under normal operating conditions (not startup/shutdown/malfunction) and include process logs/records that justify representativeness (40 CFR 63.7732(a)).

Confirm test sampling details: sampling locations (at outlet of control device or source), methods used (Method 1/1A, Method 2 family, Method 4, Method 5 or other listed methods), minimum sample volume (>=60 dscf per PM run), and number of valid runs (>=3) (40 CFR 63.7732(b)(1) and (2)).

Provide measured values needed to calculate mass-based PM emissions (if applicable): concentration (gr/dscf), volumetric flow (dscfm), mass of metal charged during each run (tons), test duration (minutes) and calculation per Equation 1 (40 CFR 63.7732(b)(6)).

Compare the reported average concentration or mass emissions rate from the test to the applicable numeric limits for a pouring station or pouring area for an existing foundry (e.g., 0.010 gr/dscf or relevant total metal HAP limits) and identify which alternative limit you are claiming (40 CFR 63.7734(a)(5)).

If asserting that the April 2005 production rates remain representative of current capabilities, compile contemporaneous production records (metal charge rates, cycles, throughput) and compare test-period production rates to current typical and maximum production rates (40 CFR 63.7732(a); 63.7732(b)(6)).

Confirm that the notification of compliance status including the performance test results was submitted within 60 days after test completion, or is planned for submission if using the test as the initial compliance demonstration (40 CFR 63.7750(e)(2)).

candidates.title: Subpart IIIII (Mercury cell chlor-alkali plants)

criteria.criterion: if the emission point is a by-product hydrogen stream or an end box ventilation system vent then you must determine weekly mercury emission rates and calculate a 52-week average mercury emission rate in g Hg/Mg Cl2 using the procedures and Equation 1 in § 63.8243(a)

if the emission point is a mercury thermal recovery unit vent and you choose the continuous monitoring option then you must calculate the daily average mercury concentration for the operating day as the average of the 15-minute CEMS readings using Equation 2 in § 63.8243(b)(1)

if the emission point is a mercury thermal recovery unit vent and you choose the periodic monitoring option then you must calculate the daily average mercury concentration using the procedures specified in § 63.8234(b) as referenced in § 63.8243(b)(2)

if you choose the continuous monitoring option for any affected vent then the mercury continuous emissions monitor must sample, analyze, and record concentrations at least once every 15 minutes and monitoring data must represent at least 75 percent of the 15-minute periods in each operating day for the compliance averaging period (excluding malfunctions, repairs, and required QA/QC)

if you choose the periodic monitoring option and your final control device is not a nonregenerable carbon adsorber then you must conduct at least three test runs per week and continuously collect data at least once every 15 minutes using a CPMS and record each 1-hour average for the applicable parameter as required in § 63.8244(b)(2)(ii)

if monitoring data are recorded during monitoring malfunctions, associated repairs, or required quality assurance or control activities then you must not use those data in averages and calculations used to report emission or operating levels or to meet minimum data availability requirements

checklist: Identify whether the emission point is a mercury thermal recovery unit vent, a by-product hydrogen stream, or an end box ventilation system vent
Document which monitoring option you will use for each emission point: continuous CEMS (§ 63.8240(a)) or periodic monitoring (§ 63.8240(b))
If continuous CEMS: confirm the monitor samples, analyzes, and records at least once every 15 minutes and meets detector sensitivity requirements (see § 63.8242(a)(1)–(2))
If continuous CEMS: verify data collection will represent ≥75% of the 15-minute periods in each operating day (excluding malfunctions/QA) for the relevant compliance averaging period
If thermal recovery unit and continuous CEMS: plan to calculate a daily operating-day average from the 15-minute readings as Equation 2 in § 63.8243(b)(1)
If thermal recovery unit and periodic monitoring: confirm procedures and calculations to be used from § 63.8234(b) as referenced in § 63.8243(b)(2)
If by-product hydrogen or end box vents: track weekly mercury emission rates and weekly chlorine production, and plan to compute the 52-week g Hg/Mg Cl2 average per Equation 1 in § 63.8243(a)
If periodic monitoring and final control device is not a nonregenerable carbon adsorber: confirm at least three test runs/week and CPMS setup to record 1-hour averages per § 63.8244(b)(2)(i)–(ii)
Confirm how monitoring malfunctions, associated repairs, and QA/QC activities will be identified and excluded from averages per § 63.8244(a)(1)–(2)
Record the compliance date specified for your affected source (see § 63.8186) to determine the start of the 52-week averaging period for by-product hydrogen/end box vents
Ensure recordkeeping procedures are in place to retain mercury emissions, daily averages, and 52-week average values as required under § 63.8246 and referenced recordkeeping sections

judge_text: {"score":2,"reason":"The answer explicitly states the requirement to calculate a daily operating‑day average for CEMS (§63.8243(b)(1)) and for periodic monitoring (§63.8243(b)(2)), and it also notes the 1‑hour CPMS averaging requirement that likely caused the confusion—so the EPA note’s two key points (daily average required; source of confusion about hourly averages) are captured."}

candidates.title: Miscellaneous Organic Chemical Manufacturing (Subpart FFFF)

criteria.criterion: If a process has batch process vents, then you must keep the records specified for each operating scenario (process description, identification of vents, applicable control requirements, control device description, vents routed to the control device, applicable monitoring requirements, calculations and engineering analyses, and reporting changes)

If your process includes batch operations, then you must maintain a schedule or log of operating scenarios for processes with batch vents and update it each time a different operating scenario is put into effect

If some Group 1 batch process vents in a process are controlled to less than the percent reduction requirement, then you must keep records of whether each batch operated was considered a standard batch and must keep estimated uncontrolled and controlled emissions for each batch considered a nonstandard batch

If you documented in your notification of compliance status that an MCPU has Group 2 batch process vents because non-reactive organic HAP is the only HAP and usage is less than 10,000 lb/yr, then you must keep records of the amount of HAP used and calculate the daily rolling annual sum of the amount used no less frequently than monthly

If you documented in your notification of compliance status that total uncontrolled organic HAP emissions from the batch process vents in an MCPU will be less than 1,000 lb/yr for the anticipated number of standard batches, then you must keep records of the number of batches operated and calculate a daily rolling annual sum of batches operated no less frequently than monthly

If you meet none of the limited-recordkeeping conditions in paragraphs (e)(1)–(3), then you must keep records of the day each batch was completed (or operating hours for continuous operations), whether each batch was a standard batch, estimated emissions for nonstandard batches, and daily 365-day rolling summations of emissions (or correlating alternative records) calculated no less frequently than monthly

If you want approval to set operating limits for parameters other than those specified in §§ 63.2455 through 63.2485 (or otherwise request approval of alternative compliance elements such as operating-limit-related recordkeeping), then you must submit a precompliance report requesting approval under § 63.2520(c) and the Administrator will approve or disapprove within 90 days

If you request approval to establish operating limits or other changes to initial compliance demonstrations, then the precompliance report must include the description of test conditions, data, calculations, and other information used to establish those operating limits as specified in § 63.2520(c)(3)

If any element specified in the operating-scenario record (other than paragraph (b)(5) listing of vents routed to a control device) is changed and was not previously reported, then that change constitutes a new operating scenario for reporting purposes

If you make process changes that are not within the scope of an existing operating scenario, then you must document the change in your compliance report or, for certain changes, provide advance notice as required in § 63.2520(e)(10)

If you elect to comply with emissions averaging for batch process vents, then estimate uncontrolled emissions for a standard batch using the procedures specified for standard-batch emissions and multiply the calculated emissions per batch by the number of batches per month when calculating monthly emissions for debits and credits

checklist: Confirm whether the subject process is an MCPU and whether emissions are from batch process vents (per the Subpart FFFF batch process vent definition).

Determine Group status of batch process vents by summing uncontrolled organic HAP emissions for the process and comparing to Group 1/Group 2 thresholds (e.g., ≥10,000 lb/yr for Group 1 at existing sources).
Identify and document your current "standard batch" operating scenario(s) (operating ranges, which conditions produce the highest emissions, and whether multiple standard-batch definitions are used).
Count historical number of batches and calculate current daily rolling 365-day emissions or batch totals used in Annual Emissions Inventory and SARA 313 reporting.
Verify whether only non-reactive organic HAP are used and whether annual usage is under 10,000 lb/yr (to assess eligibility for the Group 2 usage option).
Check whether you previously filed a Notification of Compliance Status documenting Group 2 status or other precompliance determinations relevant to reduced recordkeeping under §63.2525(e).

Decide whether you intend to request an approval (precompliance report) to set alternative operating limits or alternative recordkeeping/monitoring approaches and gather the test conditions, monitoring data, calculations, and rationale to include in that precompliance report.
Determine whether any batch vents are controlled to less than the percent reduction requirement (which triggers the standard/nonstandard batch recordkeeping in §63.2525(d)).

Identify how standard-batch-based emission estimates would be converted to monthly and annual emission totals (e.g., emissions per standard batch × number of batches per month) for consistency with inventory and SARA 313 methods.

Prepare documentation of any planned changes to operating scenarios so you can report them as new operating scenarios if they are not within the scope of existing scenarios (and note timing/advance-notice requirements in §63.2520(e)(10)).

OUR ANSWER does include the precompliance/approval pathway under §63.2520(c) for alternative operating limits/recordkeeping, but it does not cite or reference §63.10(f) (the general provision EPA cited). Thus only some of the EPA’s key reasoning is captured."}

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Pharmaceuticals Production (Subpart GGG)

criteria.criterion: if a material produced at the facility meets the definition of a "pharmaceutical product" in §63.1251 (for example: a material described by SIC code 2833 or 2834; a material whose manufacturing process is described by NAICS 325411 or 325412; a finished dosage form; an active ingredient or precursor produced at a facility whose primary operations are described by SIC 2833 or 2834; or, at a facility whose primary operations are not 2833/2834, a material whose primary use is as an active ingredient or precursor) then the operations are subject to Subpart GGG

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Miscellaneous Organic Chemical Manufacturing (MON Rule, Subpart FFFF)

criteria.criterion: if you own or operate miscellaneous organic chemical manufacturing process units (MCPU) that are located at, or are part of, a major source of HAP then those units are subject to this subpart

if a process unit satisfies all conditions in §63.2435(b) (it produces materials described in §63.2435(b)(1), it processes/uses/generates any of the organic HAP listed in section 112(b) or hydrogen halide/halogen HAP per §63.2435(b)(2), and it is not an affected source or part of an affected source under another applicable subpart per §63.2435(b)(3)) then that unit is an MCPU and is subject to Subpart FFFF

if the operations are specifically listed in the exemptions at §63.2435(c)(1) through (7) (for example research and development facilities or other enumerated exemptions) then those operations are not subject to this subpart

if the process, equipment, or collection of equipment functions as a "miscellaneous organic chemical manufacturing process" as defined in §63.2550 (i.e., all equipment which collectively function to produce a product or isolated intermediate that are materials described in §63.2435(b)) then it is treated as an MCPU for purposes of this subpart

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hydrochloric Acid (HCl) Production (Subpart NNNNN)

criteria.criterion: if you own or operate an HCl production facility that produces a liquid HCl product at a concentration of 30 weight percent or greater during its normal operations and the facility is located at, or part of, a major source of HAP then the HCl production facility is subject to Subpart NNNNN

if the facility only produces liquid HCl product at a concentration of 30 weight percent or greater only occasionally (not during normal operations) then it is not subject to Subpart NNNNN under §63.8985(a)
if the HCl production facility is also subject to any of the listed NESHAP subparts in §63.8985(b) (including Subpart GGG) then the HCl production facility is not subject to Subpart NNNNN

if all gaseous streams containing HCl and chlorine (Cl2) from HCl process vents, HCl storage tanks, and HCl transfer operations are recycled or routed to another process for a process purpose prior to discharge to the atmosphere, then the HCl production facility is not subject to Subpart NNNNN under §63.8985(f)

checklist: Confirm the identity of the product(s) you make (is the product glucosamine hydrochloride?) and record whether the product is sold or intended as a pharmaceutical active ingredient, precursor, finished dosage form, or as a non-pharmaceutical (e.g., dietary supplement, commodity chemical).

Determine the facility's primary SIC and NAICS codes and whether the facility's primary manufacturing operations are described by SIC 2833 or 2834 or NAICS 325411/325412 (per §63.1251 and §63.2435(b)(1)).

Verify whether the glucosamine hydrochloride (or intermediates/precursors) are used as an active ingredient or precursor and whether the material's primary use is pharmaceutical (per §63.1251 criteria (1)-(5)).

Establish whether you operate any miscellaneous organic chemical manufacturing process units (MCPU) as defined in §63.2550 (document the equipment that collectively functions to produce the material and whether it matches §63.2435(b)(1) product descriptions).

Calculate annual and potential-to-emit HAP totals to determine if the plant is a major source of HAP (≥10 tpy single HAP or ≥25 tpy combined HAP) as required to trigger Subpart FFFF applicability (§63.2435(a)).
Identify whether the process uses, generates, or handles organic HAP or hydrogen halide/halogen HAP (e.g., HCl) in quantities meeting §63.2435(b)(2) thresholds or definitions.

Determine whether you produce liquid HCl at ≥30 wt% during normal operations, whether that HCl is produced on-site (i.e., an HCl production unit where a gaseous stream containing HCl enters the HCl production unit), or whether you only consume/handle purchased HCl (per §63.8985(a)).

If you handle HCl, document whether HCl streams are recycled/routed for process purpose (per §63.8985(f)) or whether storage tanks are dedicated feedstock tanks excluded from the HCl production facility definition (per §63.8985(a)(2)).
Check whether any of the exemptions in §63.2435(c)(1)-(7) apply to your operations (e.g., bona fide R&D facility, listed NAICS exemptions).
Check whether the HCl production activity is already covered by other NESHAP listed in §63.8985(b) (including Subpart GGG) which would exclude Subpart NNNNN applicability.

Collect process descriptions, mass balances, and process flow diagrams showing where HCl is introduced, generated, or emitted, and quantify vent and wastewater streams (to evaluate process-vent, storage, transfer, and wastewater applicability under Subparts GGG and FFFF).

candidates.title: Site Remediation (Subpart GGGGG)

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate a facility at which you conduct a site remediation (as defined in 40 CFR 63.7957) and the site remediation cleans up a remediation material, is co-located at your facility with one or more other stationary sources that emit HAP and meet an affected-source definition regulated by another subpart under 40 CFR part 63, and your facility is a major source of HAP as defined in §63.2, then the site remediation is subject to this subpart.
If your site remediation only cleans up material that does not contain any of the HAP listed in Table 1 of this subpart, then the site remediation is not subject to this subpart.
If the site remediation is conducted at a gasoline service station to clean up remediation material from a leaking underground storage tank, then the site remediation is not subject to this subpart.
If the site remediation is conducted at a farm or residential site, then the site remediation is not subject to this subpart.
If the site remediation is conducted at a research and development facility that meets the requirements under CAA section 112(c)(7), then the site remediation is not subject to this subpart.

If the total quantity of the HAP listed in Table 1 contained in remediation material excavated, extracted, pumped, or otherwise removed during all site remediations conducted at your facility is less than 1 megagram (Mg) annually, then the site remediation activities are not subject to the requirements of this subpart except for the recordkeeping requirement in §63.7881(c)(2).

If all remediation activities at your facility subject to this subpart are completed and you have notified the Administrator in writing that all remediation activities subject to this subpart are completed, then those remediation activities are not subject to the requirements of this subpart (but records must be maintained as specified).
If a site remediation is completed within 30 consecutive calendar days according to the conditions in §63.7884(b), then the site remediation is not subject to the standards specified in §63.7884(a).

If an affected source for your site includes process vents, remediation material management units, equipment leaks meeting specified conditions, or pressure relief devices as described in §63.7882(a)(1)–(4), then those sources are subject to this subpart as affected sources.

If an equipment component contains or contacts remediation material having a concentration of total HAP listed in Table 1 equal to or greater than 10 percent by weight and is intended to operate 300 hours or more during a calendar year in remediation material service, then that equipment component is part of the equipment-leaks affected source subject to this subpart.

If a remediation material management unit is part of an affected source designated by §63.7882, then you must select and meet one of the control or management options in §63.7886(b) for that unit unless the unit is exempted under §63.7886(c) or (d).

If the average total VOHAP concentration of the remediation material managed in a remediation material management unit is less than 500 ppmw (demonstrated per §63.7943), then that remediation material management unit meets the requirements of §63.7886(b)(2) and is not required to meet the control options in §63.7886(b)(1) for that material stream.

If one or a combination of remediation material management units are designated exempt and the total annual quantity of HAP in the remediation material placed in those exempted units is less than 1 Mg/yr and you satisfy the marking/notification and documentation requirements, then those units are exempted from the requirements of §63.7886(b).

checklist: Determine whether the planned excavation/backfill activity qualifies as "site remediation" per 40 CFR 63.7957 (does the activity remove, destroy, degrade, transform, immobilize, or otherwise manage contaminated soil?).
Test representative soil samples for the HAP listed in Table 1 of Subpart GGGGG and calculate the total HAP mass removed annually to determine if the facility-wide total is >= or < 1 Mg/yr.
Determine the average total VOHAP concentration (ppmw) of the excavated soil using Method 305 or an approved alternative per §63.7943 to see if it is <500 ppmw.

Establish whether the excavated/staged-on-site soil is a "remediation material management unit" (e.g., container, surface impoundment, pile) under §63.7957 and whether those units will be managed as tanks, containers, surface impoundments, separators, or transfer systems.
Confirm whether your facility is a major source of HAP (>=10 tpy single HAP or >=25 tpy combined HAP) for applicability under §63.7881(a)(3).

Confirm whether your facility is co-located with one or more stationary sources that emit HAP and meet an affected-source definition regulated by another 40 CFR part 63 subpart (applicability element in §63.7881(a)(2)).
If using temporary on-site storage or containers, document the dates of initiation and completion of remediation actions to evaluate the 30-consecutive-day exemption per §63.7884(b).

If planning to exempt specific remediation material management units, calculate and document the annual HAP placed in those exempt units and follow the marking or notification and documentation requirements in §63.7886(d).

If equipment (pumps, valves, etc.) will contact the remediation material, determine whether any components contain >=10% total Table 1 HAP by weight and will operate >=300 hours/year to assess equipment-leak affected-source inclusion per §63.7882(a)(3).
Check whether the site/remediation scenario falls under any categorical exemptions (gasoline service station UST cleanup, farm/residential site, or qualifying R&D facility) in §63.7881(b)(4)–(6).
Prepare and retain written documentation/methodology supporting any 1 Mg determination and any VOHAP concentration measurements as required by §63.7881(c)(2) and §63.7886(d)(2).

These criteria capture the EPA rationale."}

candidates.title: Organic Liquid Distribution (OLD) (non-gasoline) operations

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate an organic liquid distribution (OLD) operation that is located at, or is part of, a major source of hazardous air pollutants (HAP) then the operation is subject to this subpart.
If the organic liquid distribution operations are located at a research and development facility consistent with CAA section 112(c)(7) then the operations are not subject to this subpart.

If the activities and equipment used to process, store, or transfer organic liquids are at oil and natural gas production field facilities or at natural gas transmission and storage facilities (as defined in the cited subparts) then those activities and equipment are not included in this subpart's coverage.

If the collection of activities and equipment used to distribute organic liquids into, out of, or within a major source facility includes storage tanks, transfer racks, equipment leak components associated with specified tanks/racks/pipelines, transport vehicles while loading/unloading at transfer racks, or containers while loading/unloading at transfer racks, then those items comprise the affected source for this subpart.

If storage tanks, transfer racks, transport vehicles, containers, or equipment leak components are part of an affected source regulated under another 40 CFR part 63 NESHAP then those items are excluded from the affected source for this subpart.

If storage tanks, transfer racks, transport vehicles, containers, or equipment leak components are non‑permanent and are used only in special‑situation distribution loading and unloading operations (such as maintenance or upset liquids management) then those items are excluded from the affected source for this subpart.

If the collection of transfer racks at your facility meets the total actual annual facility‑level organic liquid loading volume criterion for control in Table 2 (items 7 through 10) then the transfer racks must comply with the transfer rack requirements of this subpart.
If the affected source is an existing affected source then the transfer rack requirements apply during the loading of organic liquids into transport vehicles only.
If the affected source is a new affected source then the transfer rack requirements apply during the loading of organic liquids into transport vehicles and into containers.

If the liquid being stored or transferred does not meet the subpart's definition of “organic liquid” (including the listed exclusions such as gasoline, kerosene, diesel, certain fuels, hazardous waste, wastewater, ballast water, or non‑crude/non‑condensate liquids with annual average true vapor pressure < 0.7 kPa) then the requirements of this subpart do not apply to that liquid.

checklist: Determine whether the plant is a major source of HAP (to trigger applicability under §63.2334(a)).
Identify whether the operations in question are part of an OLD operation (activities to store or transfer organic liquids into, out of, or within the plant site).
Confirm whether the facility or specific equipment is a research and development facility (exclusion under §63.2334(b)).

Verify whether the activities/equipment are located at oil and natural gas production field facilities or natural gas transmission and storage facilities as defined in the referenced subparts (exclusion under §63.2334(c)).
Determine whether the containers/transfer equipment in your transfers are non‑permanent and used only for special‑situation distribution loading/unloading (maintenance/upset) per §63.2338(c)(2).

Verify whether any storage tanks, transfer racks, transport vehicles, containers, or leak components are already part of an affected source under another 40 CFR part 63 NESHAP (exclusion under §63.2338(c)(1)).
Establish whether the transfers occur at transfer racks as defined in §63.2406 (i.e., a single system used to load/unload transport vehicles or containers).

Determine whether the facility’s total actual annual facility‑level organic liquid loading volume meets or exceeds the Table 2 thresholds (items 7–10) that trigger transfer rack control per §63.2346(b).
Determine whether the affected source is new, reconstructed, or existing (see §63.2338(d)-(f)) because new vs existing affects whether loading into containers is covered (§63.2346(b)).

Confirm that the liquids being transferred meet the subpart’s “organic liquid” definition (contain ≥5% by weight organic HAP or are qualifying crude/condensate and are not among the listed exclusions) per §63.2406.

Document whether the transfers are container‑to‑container or truck‑to‑container and whether they occur while the container/transport vehicle is at a transfer rack that is part of the affected source (containers and transport vehicles are included only when loading/unloading at transfer racks per §63.2338(b)(4)-(5) and §63.2346(b)).

candidates.title: Subpart MM

criteria.criterion: if you operate a kraft or soda smelt dissolving tank equipped with a wet scrubber then you must install, calibrate, maintain, and operate a continuous parameter monitoring system (CPMS) that can determine and record the pressure drop across the scrubber and the scrubbing liquid flow rate at least once every successive 15-minute period
if you monitor pressure drop with a CPMS then the monitoring device must be certified by the manufacturer to be accurate to within a gage pressure of ±500 pascals (±2 inches of water)

if you wish to establish operating limits for the CPMS parameters then those limits must be established during the initial or periodic performance test or be based on values recorded during previous performance tests obtained using the test methods and procedures required in this subpart

if your smelt dissolving tank uses a dynamic wet scrubber that operates at ambient pressure or a low-energy entrainment scrubber where fan speed does not vary then you may use fan amperage or fan RPM measurements as an alternative to pressure drop measurement

if any 3-hour average scrubber parameter value is below the minimum operating limit established in paragraph (j) during times spent pulping liquor is fed then that is a monitoring exceedance with the exception that pressure drop is excepted during periods of startup and shutdown

candidates.title: Subpart TTTTT

criteria.criterion: if a wet scrubber is applied to meet any particulate matter, PM10, chlorine, hydrochloric acid, or dioxins/furans emission limit in Table 1 to this subpart then you must maintain the hourly average pressure drop and scrubber liquid flow rate at or above the minimum level established during the initial or subsequent performance test

if a wet scrubber is subject to operating limits for pressure drop and scrubber water flow rate then you must use the CPMS to measure and record pressure drop and scrubber water flow rate at least every 15 minutes during each run of the particulate matter performance test and set the operating limits as the lowest average individual run value among the three runs that meet the applicable emission limit

if you want to change (revise) the operating limits for a control device covered by this subpart then you must submit written notification to the Administrator, conduct a new performance test to demonstrate compliance with the applicable emission limitation, and establish revised operating limits according to the applicable procedures

if your wet scrubber is subject to the operating limits for pressure drop and scrubber water flow rates in § 63.9890(b) then you must at all times monitor the hourly average pressure drop and liquid flow rate using a CPMS according to the requirements in § 63.9921(a)

candidates.title: Subpart RRRRR

criteria.criterion: if a wet scrubber is subject to performance testing in § 63.9620 and operating limits for pressure drop and scrubber water flow rate in § 63.9590(b)(1) then you must measure and record pressure drop and scrubber water flow rate every 15 minutes during each run of the particulate matter performance test and establish site-specific operating limits as the lowest average pressure drop and lowest average scrubber water flow rate corresponding to any of the three test runs

if a rod-deck venturi scrubber is applied to an indurating furnace to meet a particulate matter emission limit then you may establish a lower average pressure drop operating limit by using historical average pressure drop data from a certified performance test completed on or after December 18, 2002, provided the corresponding average PM concentration from that historical test is at or below the applicable emission limit

if you want to change the operating limits for any air pollution control device covered by this section then you may do so only if you submit written notification to the Administrator of your request, conduct a performance test to demonstrate compliance with the applicable emission limitation, and establish revised operating limits according to the applicable procedures

checklist: Determine which NESHAP subpart(s) cover your smelt dissolving tank (Subpart MM, Subpart TTTTT, Subpart RRRRR) by confirming the source category and whether your unit appears in the applicable subpart Table 1 listings.

Confirm whether the scrubbing system is a wet scrubber (dynamic wet scrubber, low-energy entrainment scrubber, or other) and whether it is used to meet PM, PM10, chlorine, HCl, or dioxins/furans limits.

Verify whether an initial or prior performance test was performed under the applicable subpart and obtain the complete test reports and the 1-hour or run-average pressure drop and scrubber liquid flow rate values from each test run.

Confirm that any prior performance test data you intend to use were obtained using the test methods and procedures required by the applicable subpart and that no control techniques or processes have been modified since that testing (you must be able to certify no modifications).

If you intend to use fan amperage or RPM instead of pressure drop, verify your scrubber type (dynamic at ambient pressure or low-energy entrainment with constant fan speed) and collect no-load and test-run fan amperage or RPM data per the referenced procedures.

Check that your CPMS measures and records pressure drop and liquid flow at the required frequency (at least once every 15 minutes or hourly averages as required) and that the pressure-drop sensor is certified accurate to ±500 pascals (±2 inches water).

Assemble any historical certified performance test data (date of test, measured PM and corresponding pressure drop averages) if you plan to use historical values (note the December 18, 2002 cutoff specified for certain RRRRR rod-deck venturi scrubbers).

If you propose revised operating limits (lower pressure-drop setpoint), prepare to notify the Administrator and, if required by the applicable subpart, conduct a new performance test demonstrating compliance prior to establishing the revised limits.

Identify how you will compute operating limits (lowest average of the three compliant runs or other method allowed by the applicable subpart) and ensure you can produce the 15-minute CPMS data and computed run averages used to set the limit.
Document startup/shutdown procedures and understand that pressure-drop excursions during startup/shutdown may be treated differently for exceedance counting per the applicable subpart provisions.

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants for Steel Pickling and Hydrochloric Acid Regeneration Plants (Subpart CCC)

criteria.criterion: If a wet scrubber is used as the emission control device then the owner or operator must install, operate, and maintain systems to measure and record scrubber makeup water flow rate and, if the scrubber operates with recirculation, recirculation water flow rate, with those flow rates monitored continuously and recorded at least once per shift while the scrubber is operating.

If a performance test is conducted for a wet scrubber then the owner or operator must establish site-specific minimum scrubber makeup water flow rate and, for scrubbers with recirculation, minimum recirculation water flow rate, and during the emission test monitor each operating parameter continuously and record them with sufficient frequency to establish a representative average but no less frequently than once every 15 minutes.

If scrubber makeup water flow rate or recirculation water flow rate excursions occur below the minimum values established during performance testing then the owner or operator must initiate corrective action as specified by the subpart's maintenance requirements.

If a monitoring device is used to measure the required operating parameters then each monitoring device must be certified by the manufacturer to be accurate to within 5 percent and must be calibrated in accordance with the manufacturer's instructions but not less frequently than once per year.
If the owner or operator fails to record each of the operating parameters listed for wet scrubbers then that failure is a violation of the monitoring requirements of this subpart.

If a wet scrubber is used then the owner or operator shall maintain records of scrubber makeup water flow rate and recirculation water flow rate for 5 years and keep the most recent 2 years of records on site.

If a performance test is used to demonstrate compliance then performance tests to measure HCl mass flows at the control device inlet and outlet or HCl concentration must be conducted either annually or on an alternative schedule approved by the permitting authority but no less frequently than every 2 1/2 years or twice per title V permit term.

If an operation uses a scrubber emission control device then the operation and maintenance plan must require monitoring and recording the pressure drop across the scrubber once per shift while the scrubber is operating.

If an affected hydrochloric acid regeneration plant is subject to this subpart then the owner or operator must install, operate, and maintain systems to measure and record process offgas temperature (monitored continuously and recorded at least once every shift while in production mode) and parameters used to determine proportion of excess air (determined and recorded at least once every shift while in production mode).

checklist: Confirm whether each control device on each continuous pickling line and the acid regeneration plant is a wet scrubber or another type of control device.
For each scrubber, confirm whether the scrubber operates with recirculation (yes/no).
Obtain the site-specific minimum makeup water flow rate and minimum recirculation water flow rate established during the most recent performance test for each scrubber.
Verify that flow measurement instruments for scrubber makeup and recirculation water are installed and specified to monitor continuously.
Obtain manufacturer certification that each monitoring device is accurate to within 5 percent for each installed flow meter.
Verify calibration records showing each monitoring device was calibrated at least once in the last 12 months per manufacturer's instructions.
Verify that flow rates are recorded at least once per shift while each scrubber is operating (and identify the shift schedule used to determine 'once per shift').

For any recent performance test, verify that operating parameters were recorded at least once every 15 minutes during the emission test runs and that the compliant monitoring values were determined as averages of those records.
Confirm the schedule and records for performance tests (annual or alternative approved schedule, but no less frequently than every 2.5 years or twice per title V permit term).

Confirm whether procedures to initiate corrective action are documented in the operation and maintenance plan and note the timeline for initiation (e.g., within 1 working day) and completion of corrective actions.

Verify that the operation and maintenance plan includes monitoring/recording of scrubber pressure drop once per shift and the inspection/maintenance tasks required for scrubbers (cleaning, inspections at intervals no less than 3 months, etc.).

Confirm that records of scrubber makeup and recirculation flow rates, calibration and manufacturer certifications, and maintenance/inspection records are retained for 5 years and that the most recent 2 years of records are maintained on site.

If operating an acid regeneration plant, verify that process offgas temperature is monitored continuously and recorded at least once every shift while in production mode and that parameters used to determine proportion of excess air are measured and recorded at least once every shift while in production mode.

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants: Miscellaneous Coating Manufacturing

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate miscellaneous coating manufacturing operations that (1) are located at or are part of a major source of hazardous air pollutants (HAP) emissions, (2) manufacture coatings as defined in §63.8105, (3) process, use, or produce HAP, and (4) are not part of an affected source under another subpart of part 63, then the operations are subject to the requirements in this subpart.
If a unit is a process vessel as described in §63.7985(b)(1), then that unit is included in the miscellaneous coating manufacturing affected source.

If a process vessel at an existing affected source is stationary and has a capacity greater than or equal to 250 gallons, then it may be eligible to elect the emissions‑averaging alternative for stationary process vessels in §63.8050.

If a process vessel has a capacity less than 250 gallons, then it is not eligible for the emissions‑averaging alternative that applies to stationary process vessels greater than or equal to 250 gallons in §63.8050(a).

If cleaning emissions are from automatic cleaning operations, then the emission limits and work practice standards in Table 1 to this subpart apply, and if the cleaning is conducted manually, then those Table 1 emission limits and work practice standards do not apply to the cleaning emissions.

If the operation is described in any of the exclusions in §63.7985(d)(1)–(5) (for example research and development facilities or affiliated operations covered under listed other subparts), then the requirements for miscellaneous coating manufacturing in this subpart do not apply to that operation.

checklist: Is the facility a major source of HAP as defined in CAA section 112(a)?
Does the mixer perform operations that "manufacture coatings" as defined in §63.8105 (e.g., mixing raw coating ingredients to produce a coating product)?
Does the mixer process, use, or produce any HAP-containing materials? (Identify specific HAP and concentrations.)
Is the 125‑gallon mixer used as a process vessel (i.e., used for mixing/processing coating ingredients) rather than solely as ancillary equipment?
Is the mixer considered stationary at your affected source or truly portable/temporary for regulatory purposes?
Is the mixer part of an affected source covered by another Part 63 subpart (e.g., affiliated operations under the subparts listed in §63.7985(d)(2))?
Is the mixer located at a research and development facility as defined in CAA §112(c)(7)?
Are cleaning operations for the mixer automatic or manual?
Do you plan to use the emissions‑averaging alternative (note: averaging groups apply only to stationary vessels ≥250 gallons)?
If considering emissions averaging: confirm vessel capacity (≥250 gal) and whether all vessels in the averaging group have tightly‑fitting vented covers per §63.8050(b)(2).

If emissions are routed to control devices or condensers, document whether emissions go to closed‑vent systems and the type of control device (condenser vs other) to determine how to estimate controlled emissions per §63.8050(c).
If electing averaging, prepare uncontrolled and controlled emissions estimates (pounds per batch) and a monthly batch production log to support continuous compliance per §63.8050(c) and (d).

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants: Site Remediation (Subpart GGGGG)

criteria.criterion: If you own or operate a facility at which you conduct a site remediation (as defined in 40 CFR 63.7957) and that site remediation (a) cleans up a remediation material, (b) is co-located at your facility with one or more other stationary sources that emit HAP and meet an affected source definition specified for a source category regulated by another subpart of 40 CFR part 63, and (c) your facility is a major source of HAP as defined in §63.2, then this subpart applies to you.
If your site remediation only cleans up material that does not contain any of the HAP listed in Table 1 of this subpart, then your site remediation is not subject to this subpart.

If your site remediation is conducted at a gasoline service station to clean up remediation material from a leaking underground storage tank, then your site remediation is not subject to this subpart.
If your site remediation is conducted at a farm or residential site, then your site remediation is not subject to this subpart.
If your site remediation is conducted at a research and development facility that meets the requirements under CAA section 112(c)(7), then your site remediation is not subject to this subpart.

If the total quantity of the HAP listed in Table 1 contained in the remediation material excavated, extracted, pumped, or otherwise removed during all of the site remediations conducted at your facility is less than 1 megagram (Mg) annually and you prepare and maintain written documentation of the methodology and data used, then your site remediation activities are not subject to the requirements of this subpart except for the recordkeeping requirement.

If all remediation activities at your facility subject to this subpart are completed and you have notified the Administrator in writing that all remediation activities subject to this subpart are completed, then your site remediation is not subject to the requirements of this subpart (subject to maintaining records of compliance).

If a unit at your site is a process vent, a remediation material management unit (tank, surface impoundment, container, oil-water separator, organic-water separator, or transfer system), an equipment component that contains or contacts remediation material with total HAP ≥ 10 percent by weight and is intended to operate in remediation material service for 300 hours or more per year, or a pressure relief device in remediation material service, then that unit is an affected source subject to this subpart.

If you commenced construction or reconstruction of the affected source before July 30, 2002 (or under CERCLA/RCRA conditions described for dates on or before May 13, 2016), then the affected source is considered an existing source; if commenced on or after those dates (or under CERCLA/RCRA after May 13, 2016 where specified), then it is considered a new source as specified in this section.

If the remediation units are located on property that is not under common control (i.e., not owned, leased, or operated by the same entity, parent, or subsidiary), then those units are part of a different facility and are not part of your facility for purposes of this subpart's applicability.

checklist: Do you (the current owner/operator) own or operate the remediation units, or are they owned/operated by another legal entity?

Are the remediation units on property that is under common control with your facility (owned, leased, or operated by the same entity, parent, or subsidiary) per the facility definition in 40 CFR 63.7957?
Do you conduct site remediation activities as defined in 40 CFR 63.7957 (activities to remove/destroy/degrade/transform/immobilize remediation material, not mere monitoring)?
Does the remediation material contain any HAP listed in Table 1 of Subpart GGGGG?
What is the total annual quantity (mass) of the HAPs in remediation material excavated/extracted/pumped/removed during all site remediations at your facility (facility-wide, in megagrams per year)?
Do you have written documentation (methodology and data) supporting the calculation of total HAP quantity in remediation materials, as required by 40 CFR 63.7881(c)(2)?
Is the site remediation co-located with one or more other stationary sources at your facility that emit HAP and meet an affected source definition under another subpart of 40 CFR part 63?
Is your facility a major source of HAP (PTE ≥10 tpy for any single HAP or ≥25 tpy combined), using the definition in 40 CFR 63.2?

Are any of the remediation units process vents, tanks/surface impoundments/containers/oil-water or organic-water separators, transfer systems, equipment components, or pressure relief devices as defined in 40 CFR 63.7957?

For equipment components: does the component contain or contact remediation material with total HAP ≥10 percent by weight, and is it intended to operate in remediation material service for ≥300 hours/year?
When were construction or reconstruction activities for the affected remediation sources commenced (dates relative to July 30, 2002 and May 13, 2016 for CERCLA/RCRA exceptions)?
Is the remediation activity covered by an exemption category (gasoline service station leaking UST, farm/residential site, or R&D meeting CAA section 112(c)(7))?
Have you (or the remediation owner/operator) notified the Administrator in writing that all remediation activities subject to this subpart are completed (if applicable)?
Does your Title V permit include (or will it include at renewal/reopening) any recordkeeping required under 40 CFR 63.7881(c)(2) or other conditions required by this subpart?

candidates.title: Hazardous Waste Combustors (Subpart EEE)

criteria.criterion: If the rotary kiln and the secondary combustion chamber are separate areas in which controlled flame combustion of hazardous waste occurs, then each is a combustion chamber.

If a hazardous waste combustor has more than one combustion chamber, then you must measure the temperature of each combustion chamber and establish a minimum hourly rolling average combustion chamber temperature limit for each chamber based on the average of the performance test run averages.

If a minimum combustion chamber temperature operating parameter limit is established under § 63.1209, then the automatic waste feed cutoff (AWFCO) must immediately and automatically cut off the hazardous waste feed when that limit is exceeded and you may not ramp down pumpable waste feed when the AWFCO is triggered by a minimum combustion chamber temperature exceedance.

If you plan to change the design, operation, or maintenance (for example, to treat multiple combustion chambers as one) in a manner that may adversely affect compliance, then you must notify the Administrator at least 60 days prior, include a comprehensive performance test schedule and plan, conduct comprehensive performance testing to document compliance and establish operating parameter limits, submit a Notification of Compliance, and limit hazardous waste burning to the hours allowed prior to submitting the Notification unless the Administrator approves otherwise.

If you seek to waive an operating parameter limit (such as minimum combustion chamber temperature), then you must submit an application to the Administrator with the comprehensive performance test plan including data and justification showing the limit is not needed or an alternative monitoring requirement that provides equivalent or better assurance of compliance, and the Administrator will approve only if those criteria are met.

checklist: Determine whether the rotary kiln and the secondary combustion chamber are physically and functionally distinct areas in which controlled flame combustion of hazardous waste occurs (i.e., separate flame zones, separate gas flow paths).

Identify how 'combustion chamber' was defined and documented in your most recent comprehensive performance test plan and Notification of Compliance (location(s) of temperature sensors specified in the test plan).

Confirm whether minimum combustion chamber temperature operating parameter limits were established for each chamber in the Documentation of Compliance or Notification of Compliance and record the numeric limits and averaging periods.

Check whether temperature monitoring points (thermocouples/pyrometers) exist for each chamber and whether they represent the bulk gas temperature in the combustion zone as documented in the test plan.
Verify whether the minimum combustion chamber temperature OPL(s) are interlocked to the AWFCO (check control logic and interlock configuration).

If you intend to treat the two chambers as one for OPL purposes, assemble data demonstrating that a single temperature limit or alternative monitoring would provide equivalent assurance of compliance and include that data in the comprehensive performance test plan for submittal to the Administrator.

If you have modified or plan to modify design/operation to treat chambers as one, confirm whether the change is a 'change' under § 63.1206(b)(5) and, if so, prepare the 60-day notification, comprehensive test schedule/plan, and be prepared to limit hazardous waste burning per § 63.1206(b)(5)(i)(C) until Notification of Compliance is submitted or Administrator approval obtained.

Review historical comprehensive performance test records to determine whether DRE and dioxin/furan tests measured temperatures separately for each chamber and whether limits derived from those tests covered one or both chambers.
Calculate and document hazardous waste residence time (per 40 CFR 63.1206(b)(11) / 63.1201 definition) to determine when OPLs apply and whether waste remains in the system across chambers.

If pursuing an operating parameter waiver or alternative monitoring, confirm timing (application must be submitted with the comprehensive performance test plan) and include the required justification, data, and proposed alternative monitoring approach per § 63.1209(g).

judge_text: {"score":2, "reason":"The EPA Notes key reason—that the rotary kiln and secondary combustion chamber are separate combustion chambers and thus each must have its own minimum combustion chamber temperature OPL—is directly captured by the answer: criteria and checklist explicitly address (1) determining separateness of chambers and (2) the rule requirement to measure and establish a minimum temperature limit for each combustion chamber (with appropriate citations)."}

candidates.title: Surface Coating of Metal Furniture

criteria.criterion: if you own or operate a new, reconstructed, or existing affected source used for surface coating of metal furniture and that source is a major source, is located at a major source, or is part of a major source of emissions of hazardous air pollutants then you are subject to this subpart
if the surface coating conducted at an affected source uses only coatings, thinners, and cleaning materials that contain no organic HAP then the surface coating is not subject to this subpart

if the surface coating of metal components of wood furniture is conducted in an operation that is subject to the wood furniture manufacturing NESHAP in subpart JJ then the surface coating is not subject to this subpart
if the surface coating occurs at research or laboratory facilities or is part of janitorial, building, and facility maintenance operations then the surface coating is not subject to this subpart

if the surface coating is of only small items such as knobs, hinges, or screws that have a wider use beyond metal furniture and the surface coating does not occur at an affected metal furniture source then the surface coating is not subject to this subpart

if the surface coating is conducted for the purpose of repairing or maintaining metal furniture used by a major source and not for commerce, and organic HAP emissions from the surface coating itself are not as high as the rates specified in paragraph (b) then the surface coating is not subject to this subpart
if the surface coating is performed on-site at installations owned or operated by the Armed Forces of the United States then the surface coating is not subject to this subpart

if the collection of items listed in § 63.4882(b) (all coating operations, storage containers and mixing vessels, conveying equipment, and waste-handling items used for surface coating of metal furniture) constitutes an affected source and that affected source is a major source then that affected source is subject to this subpart

checklist: Confirm whether the products you coat (stainless steel cabinetry) qualify as "metal furniture" (examples in 40 CFR 63.4881(a) include household, office, institutional, public building fixtures, shelving, lockers, lighting fixtures—document how your cabinetry fits or differs).

Determine whether your facility is a major source of HAP: calculate potential-to-emit (PTE) and actual annual emissions—is any single HAP ≥ 10.0 tpy (9.07 Mg/yr) or combined HAP ≥ 25.0 tpy (22.68 Mg/yr)?

Identify the affected source per 40 CFR 63.4882(b): list all coating operations, storage containers and mixing vessels for coatings/thinners/cleaning materials, all pumps/piping and equipment conveying those materials, and all equipment conveying waste from coating operations.

Verify whether you currently use any coatings, thinners, or cleaning materials that contain organic HAP (nonzero organic HAP mass fraction): obtain manufacturer's formulation data or test materials using methods cited in 40 CFR 63.4941(a) (e.g., Method 311 or Method 24) and calculate organic HAP content per 40 CFR 63.4941(d).

If you claim "no organic HAP" for thinners and cleaning materials, confirm that mass fraction of organic HAP equals zero for each thinner and cleaning material as determined by supplier data or testing per 40 CFR 63.4941(a).

If relying on supplier/manufacturer data for coatings, thinners, or cleaning materials, retain the supporting documentation showing organic HAP contents (manufacturer's formulation data) and ensure it meets the criteria in 40 CFR 63.4941(a)(4).

If you previously used HAP-containing adhesives or paints but have ceased, document the change and current material inventory (dates, MSDS/formulation data) to show current materials contain no organic HAP.

Confirm whether any surface coating activities are research/laboratory, janitorial/maintenance, small-item-only, repair/maintenance not for commerce, or on Armed Forces installations (see exemptions in 40 CFR 63.4881(c)(2)-(6)); document the nature and purpose of such activities.

If you determine the source is subject and you intend to use the compliant material option, verify for each coating that organic HAP content (kg organic HAP per liter coating solids) is ≤ the applicable emission limit and that all thinners and cleaning materials contain no organic HAP, using the test/data and calculation steps in 40 CFR 63.4941(a)-(d).

Keep records required to support whichever determination you rely on (material data, test reports, PTE calculations, and documentation of exemptions) as described in the subpart (see recordkeeping and reporting sections referenced in 40 CFR 63.4941(e)).

candidates.title: National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants: Secondary Lead Smelting (Subpart X)

criteria.criterion: If your facility is a secondary lead smelter (i.e., a facility at which lead-bearing scrap material is recycled into elemental lead or lead alloys by smelting) then the facility is subject to this subpart.

If you own or operate any affected source at a secondary lead smelter (including blast, reverberatory, rotary, and electric furnaces; refining kettles; agglomerating furnaces; dryers; process fugitive emissions sources; buildings containing lead-bearing materials; or fugitive dust sources) then you are subject to this subpart.
If you are a primary lead processor, lead refiner, or lead remelter then the provisions of this subpart do not apply to you.

If you are an existing source, then you must maintain lead compound concentrations in any process vent at or below 1.0 mg lead per dry standard cubic meter and must maintain the flow-weighted average concentration from all process vents at or below 0.20 mg lead per dry standard cubic meter on a 12-month rolling average basis.

If you are a new source (construction or reconstruction commenced after May 19, 2011) then you must maintain the concentration of lead compounds in any process vent gas at or below 0.20 mg lead per dry standard cubic meter.

checklist: Confirm whether your process involves smelting lead-bearing scrap into elemental lead or lead alloys (i.e., whether you meet the §63.542 definition of a secondary lead smelter).

Identify and list any equipment/processes you operate that match the 'affected source' list (blast, reverberatory, rotary, electric furnaces; refining kettles; agglomerating furnaces; dryers; process fugitive emissions sources; buildings containing lead-bearing materials; fugitive dust sources).
Determine whether your facility is a primary lead processor, lead refiner, or lead remelter (which are excluded by §63.541(a)).
Determine whether your facility is a 'new source' (construction or reconstruction commenced after May 19, 2011).

Inventory all process vents and obtain or schedule lead concentration and flow rate measurements for each vent using the referenced test methods (e.g., Method 12 or 29 and appropriate flow and gas composition methods per §63.547).
Calculate the flow-weighted average lead concentration from all process vents on a 12-month rolling average basis (using the most recent test data monthly) per §63.543(a) and Equation 1.
Verify whether any single process vent concentration exceeds 1.0 mg/dscm (existing source) or 0.20 mg/dscm (new source) as applicable per §63.543(a)–(b).

Confirm whether emissions are discharged through process vents (stacks) versus uncontrolled fugitive emissions or building ventilation, since different elements of the rule and monitoring requirements may apply.

Check whether control devices (baghouses, wet scrubbers, HEPA, wet ESP) are used and document monitoring systems in place (bag leak detection, CEMS, differential pressure monitors, temperature monitors) per §63.548.
Assemble records of construction/reconstruction dates, process descriptions, and any previous emissions test reports to support applicability determinations and required compliance calculations.

candidates.title: Subpart WW

criteria.criterion: If the owner or operator performs external floating roof (EFR) seal gap measurements, then a record shall be kept that includes the raw data obtained and any calculations performed

If records described in paragraph (a) of §63.1065 are required, then those records shall be kept for as long as the liquid is stored and records required in paragraphs (b), (c), and (d) shall be kept for at least 5 years
If records are required under §63.1065, then they shall be kept in such a manner that they can be readily accessed within 24 hours and may be kept in hard copy or computer‑readable form

candidates.title: Subpart A (General Provisions)

criteria.criterion: If an owner or operator is subject to this part, then they must maintain files of all information required by this part in a form suitable and readily available for expeditious inspection and review and retain those files for at least 5 years, with at minimum the most recent 2 years of data retained on site

If measurements or raw monitoring data are required to demonstrate compliance, then the owner or operator must retain all required measurements and raw data as specified in §63.10(b)(2) (including the subparagraphs that govern retention of CEMS/monitoring raw data)

candidates.title: Subpart HHHHHHH

criteria.criterion: If you have internal or external floating roof storage vessels subject to this subpart, then you must maintain the records required in §63.1065 of subpart WW (including records of raw data for floating roof seal gap measurements)

checklist: Identify which NESHAP subpart(s) apply to each tank (e.g., Subpart WW, Subpart HHHHHHH, Subpart DD, Subpart G) for your facility and each vessel
For each external floating roof (EFR) tank, verify whether seal gap measurements and other floating roof inspections are performed and how frequently

For each inspection/measurement, verify whether the original field data sheets include the ‘raw data’ (instrument readings, dates/times, inspector ID, and any intermediate calculation steps) versus only summary values entered later
Confirm whether the electronic entry reproduces and preserves the original raw measurement values and calculations (date/time stamps, numeric readings, calculations, and who entered/approved)
Determine for each record which retention rule applies: records under §63.1065(a) must be kept as long as the liquid is stored, while records under §63.1065(b),(c),(d) must be kept at least 5 years
Verify the physical or electronic location of records and whether the most recent 2 years of required records are kept on site and are readily accessible within 24 hours (per §63.10(b)(1))
Confirm the format of retained records (hard copy versus computer‑readable) and that electronic storage preserves required content and accessibility per §63.1065 and §63.10

If original field notes are discarded after electronic transfer, document that the electronic record contains all raw data and calculations required by §63.1065(b)(2) and §63.10(b)(2)(vii) before disposing of originals

Determine whether any state delegation or permitting authority has additional or different on‑site retention or format requirements (i.e., where to submit reports and whether State rules modify recordkeeping practices)

For each vessel, document the date the liquid began being stored (to establish any 'as long as liquid is stored' retention period) and inventory which specific records fall into the long‑term versus 5‑year retention categories
